blocks.text:
Depart at 08:00 for the Caribbean coast. After crossing to the right side of the canal via the new bridge, which opened on 2 August 2019, continue to the San Lorenzo nature reserve.

Fort San Lorenzo stands at the water's edge on a cliff about 25 metres above sea level. Built by the Spanish in 1596, the fort overlooks the Caribbean Sea and the mouth of the Chagres River.

The history of this coast is marked by Spanish conquest and pirate raids. The forts of San Lorenzo and Portobelo are linked to the stories of Francis Drake, Henry Morgan, Edward Vernon and other buccaneers.

To protect valuables, King Philip II of Spain ordered fortifications to be built along the Caribbean coast. San Lorenzo, San Jerónimo, Santiago de la Gloria, San Fernando and San Fernandín are among those that survive. In 1980, UNESCO added the 17th- and 18th-century colonial buildings and forts on Panama's Caribbean coast to the World Heritage List.

The next stop is the Agua Clara Locks on the Caribbean side of the Panama Canal. The complex began operating on 26 June 2016 and handles large Panamax and Neopanamax vessels.

As at the older locks, ships here are raised and lowered by about 26 metres relative to sea level. Agua Clara has three lock chambers. The visitor centre is set on a cliff, with a clear view of passing ships and viewing scopes for visitors. From the viewing area, you can also see Gatún Lake and ships waiting to enter the canal.

A film at the visitor centre shows how the locks were built. After the visit, return to Panama City by car. The drive takes about two hours.

**Lunch:** not included in the tour price. Your guide can recommend a restaurant.
A large body of water among wooded hills in Chagres National Park, Panama
Chagres National Park: a panoramic view of the water and forested hills

After breakfast, set out on a six-hour sightseeing tour of the capital.

Founded by conquistadors in the 16th century, Panama City became the first Spanish city and port on the Pacific coast. The tour takes in both the old city, Panamá Viejo, and the newer city.

Panamá Viejo preserves the ruins of early 17th-century cathedrals, monasteries and bridges. The tour includes the Panamá Viejo Archaeological Park and museum.

In the newer city, the focus is on Casco Antiguo, the well-preserved colonial district protected by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site. Narrow streets open onto squares and parks, and historic buildings stand alongside restored neighbourhoods.

The drive takes you through the former canal residential area where Americans involved in the canal's construction lived, then along Balboa Avenue beside Panama Bay.

Continue on foot through the historic centre. The route includes the National Theatre, one of Panama's most distinctive examples of Neoclassical architecture, as well as Plaza de Francia and San José Church. At the church, you will hear how its Golden Altar was saved and see a Nativity scene installed for Christmas 2017.

Plaza Bolívar has a monument to Simón Bolívar, a national hero in many Central and South American countries.

Next, visit Cathedral Square, where you will see the cathedral, which reopened after restoration in 2019, the Panama Canal Museum and the Municipal Palace.

The city tour ends at the Amador Causeway. Naos, Perico and Flamenco were once three separate islands in the ocean. Today the area is part of Panama City.

**Lunch:** not included in the tour price. Your guide will recommend restaurants on the day.

After the tour, transfer to the airport for your onward flight.
